Physics hand-checked: α = (R − R₀)/(R₀ Δt) = ΔR/(R₀ Δt); the fractional change is taken against the ORIGINAL resistance R₀; unit per °C (or per kelvin); the book's own form α = ΔR/(RΔt) /°C matches with R read as the original resistance.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: The temperature coefficient of resistance is
the fractional change in resistance per one
The change is compared with the original
steps.margin_note: First mark. Fractional change means change divided by the ORIGINAL resistance.
steps.why: A change of 1 Ω means little on its own — it is large for a 2 Ω wire and tiny for a 2000 Ω wire. Dividing by the original resistance makes the number a property of the material, not of the piece.
common_mistakes: Writing change in resistance per degree without dividing by R₀ — that is not fractional.
Comparing the change with the final resistance instead of the original.

recall.must_convey: That alpha is the fractional change in resistance, change divided by original resistance, per one degree rise in temperature.
accept: fractional change in resistance per degree
change in resistance by original resistance per degree rise
ratio of change to original resistance per unit temperature

steps.memory_tip: Three parts in order: change ÷ original ÷ degrees.

lines: If the resistance changes by ΔR when the
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The unit per °C completes the formula.
steps.why: ΔR/R₀ is a pure number, so dividing it by a temperature interval leaves a quantity whose unit is one over degree — per °C.
common_mistakes: Writing α = ΔR/Δt without R₀ in the denominator.

recall.must_convey: That alpha equals delta R by R naught delta t, with unit per degree celsius.
accept: alpha equals delta R by R naught delta t
delta R over R naught times delta t
reject: fractional change in resistance per degree

steps.memory_tip: α carries the two deltas: ΔR on top, R₀ Δt below.

insider_note: The word fractional and the unit per °C are the two details this definition is marked on.
